item.title: Casey Anthony Assists YNW Melly Defense Prep Ahead Of January Retrial
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: YNW Melly's legal team brought Casey Anthony into retrial preparations as a research assistant for a private investigator.
item.content:encoded:
Casey Anthony is assisting with preparation for YNW Melly‘s January 2027 double-murder retrial in Florida.

TMZ reports Anthony is working as a research assistant for private investigator Pat McKenna, whom the rapper’s law firm hired.

Her work involves researching parts of the case, although the team has not described the specific evidence or issues assigned to her.

Anthony and McKenna did not respond to the outlet’s requests for comment. YNW Melly’s legal team also did not explain how long Anthony has been involved in the preparation.

The rapper, whose legal name is Jamell Demons, faces two counts of first-degree murder in the October 26, 2018 deaths of Anthony Williams, known as YNW Sakchaser, and Christopher Thomas Jr., known as YNW Juvy.

Prosecutors allege Williams and Thomas were shot inside a vehicle and that the scene was made to look like a drive-by shooting. Demons has pleaded not guilty.

His first trial ended in a mistrial in July 2023 after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict. The retrial is set to begin January 6, 2027. Prosecutors are again seeking the death penalty if he is convicted.

Antonio Henry, known as YNW Bortlen, was charged alongside Demons. Henry pleaded guilty in September 2025 to accessory after the fact and witness tampering charges. He received a 10-year prison sentence followed by probation.

The defense added attorney Drew Findling this year. Findling joined the case after helping secure Lil Durk’s acquittal in a federal murder-for-hire trial.

AllHipHop previously reported that Findling criticized the length and conditions of Demons’ pretrial detention.

Anthony’s role connects McKenna to another high-profile criminal case. McKenna worked as a defense investigator during Anthony’s 2011 trial in Florida.

A jury acquitted her of murder, aggravated child abuse and aggravated manslaughter in the death of her daughter, Caylee.

She was convicted of four misdemeanor counts of providing false information to law enforcement, and two of those convictions were later overturned on appeal.

Demons has remained in custody since February 2019. His defense now has two months to finish its preparation before jury selection is scheduled to begin in January.

item.title: LL Cool J Credits Navy SEALs With Teaching Him Quiet Confidence
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: LL Cool J says the Navy SEALs he met for Sam Hanna showed him how humility can sit beside extraordinary skill and danger.
item.content:encoded:
LL Cool J says the real Navy SEALs he met while getting ready to play Sam Hanna taught him a clear lesson. Great skill does not always come with noise.

The rapper and actor has played a former SEAL for years on NCIS. He told Military.com that the service members he met were “extremely humble.” Yet they were also among the most dangerous people he had met.

His point was not about fear. It was about the space between what those men could do and how little they felt a need to show off.

That lesson fits the Sam Hanna now leading CBS’ NCIS: New York. Skydance’s guide to the new show says Hanna comes home after years of covert work. The death of a friend pulls him into a case with a new team. It also makes him face a city that has changed since he left.

LL Cool J’s respect for the people behind the role goes back many years. In a 2011 CBS interview, he said he went to Camp Pendleton. He spent time with Marines, sailors and special-ops troops.

“These are people that put their lives on the line every day,” he said.

That work gave him more than tips on how to move or hold a weapon. It gave him a model for Hanna’s calm and self-control. Hanna can face grave risk without turning every room into a stage.

That lines up with the quiet strength LL Cool J says he saw up close.

The actor is also still finding new sides of Hanna. The series moves him from Los Angeles back to New York.

Both the star and the role have roots there. CBS has sold the show as a new chapter, not just more of the same. The move lets fans see a man who knows his job but must learn his home again.

It is a busy time for LL Cool J. He also has his first Las Vegas run on the way and still finds time for live shows. But his latest note goes back to the base of his TV work.

Watch the people who do the job. Listen to how they carry their power. Then let that truth shape the role.

item.title: Tee Grizzley Details Mexico Detention And Alleged $70,000 Loss
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Tee Grizzley says a birthday trip to Mexico ended with three days in jail, $70,000 gone and his son's party missed.
item.content:encoded:
Tee Grizzley says a trip to Mexico for his son’s birthday ended with three days in jail, $70,000 gone and the party happening without him.

The Detroit rapper described the ordeal during a Cover Lines conversation with B.Dot. Tee said he had traveled with his wife and son when authorities found the cash in a bag.

He maintained that he had forgotten the money was there. According to his account, officials counted it, told him the matter would go to court and placed him in handcuffs.

His wife took their son away before the arrest unfolded in front of him. Tee said the timing made the detention especially painful: “The day of his party, bro, I’m still in there. And they jails over there. That ain’t where you want to be for three days.”

The interview gave Tee room to separate the Mexico episode from the older cases attached to his name. This time, the stakes he described were immediate and personal: getting back to his family, recovering the cash and dealing with a birthday he could not attend.

The episode also became music.

Tee’s album They Forgot, released September 25 through 300 Entertainment, includes a record titled “Locked Up In Mexico.” The 16-track project arrived as he was speaking more openly about the legal problems that once complicated his career.

In August, Tee celebrated having his felony record cleared.

“Every felony GONE!!!! Thank you God,” he wrote before telling supporters, “Your comeback can be greater than your setback.”

The update carried practical weight for an artist who said his record had restricted touring and business opportunities.

His Mexico story is different: it is a new account of a short detention rather than another chapter in those old Michigan cases.

For now, Tee has framed the experience through the interview and the song, with no independently reported ruling resolving what became of the $70,000.

item.title: Caitlin Clark Gets Dick’s & Foot Locker Deal
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Caitlin Clark becomes the first athlete brand partner for Dick's and Foot Locker under a new multiyear retail deal.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark has become the first athlete signed as a brand partner by both Dick’s Sporting Goods and Foot Locker.

The Indiana Fever guard agreed to an exclusive multiyear deal with the two retailers. Dick’s announced the partnership after completing its acquisition of Foot Locker last year, making Clark the first athlete to hold the role across the combined business.

“Being the first ever brand partner for both them and Foot Locker is a really special full-circle moment,” Clark said.

The deal goes far beyond a single ad. Dick’s and Foot Locker plan to feature Clark in national and global campaigns. They will also build promotions around her signature footwear, apparel and other products.

Clark is expected to appear in retail and digital experiences, fan events and community programs. Financial terms were not disclosed.

At the New York event introducing the partnership, Clark described the goal broadly. “Our vision is to connect with the greatest amount of people that we possibly can,” she said.

The timing puts the agreement next to Clark’s biggest product launch yet. Nike released her first signature basketball shoe, the Caitlin 1, worldwide on October 1. The shoe is part of an 18-piece collection that also includes performance apparel and sportswear.

Nike built the shoe around Clark’s speed, range and quick release. Clark worked closely on the design, which includes her double-Swoosh logo, No. 22 details and nods to the driveway court where she learned the game.

“I never thought I would have my own signature shoe,” Clark said when Nike unveiled the collection.

The new retail deal gives Clark two large storefront networks for that growing line. It also puts her at the center of basketball and sneaker marketing for Dick’s and Foot Locker, from product drops to fan programs.

The companies are treating her as a partner, not only a paid face. That means Clark can help shape how her products reach young players and sneaker buyers. It also gives the retailers a clear star for campaigns that connect pro basketball, youth sports and streetwear.

Clark’s reach has already changed the business around women’s basketball. This partnership shows the retailers are betting that her audience will follow her from the court to stores around the world.

item.title: Gavin Newsom Moves To Clear California Death Row With 548 Commutations
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Gavin Newsom seeks to replace 548 California death sentences with life without parole in the largest action of its kind.
item.content:encoded:
California Governor Gavin Newsom moved to commute every death sentence in the state, a sweeping action covering 548 people and potentially becoming the largest mass death-sentence commutation in United States history.

The proposed resentencings would replace execution with life in prison without the possibility of parole. Newsom’s office said the group includes 529 men and 19 women.

The change will not become final for everyone at once. Under the California Constitution, the state Supreme Court must approve clemency for people with more than one felony conviction.

The Associated Press reported that 382 of the 548 cases require that review. The other 166 commutations do not depend on that multiple-felony review.

Newsom tied the decision to his long opposition to capital punishment. He said “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values” and argued the system has failed to operate fairly.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006. Newsom imposed a moratorium shortly after taking office in 2019. The state later moved condemned prisoners out of San Quentin’s former death-row units and into the general prison population.

The scale reaches beyond California. The Marshall Project calculated that the move could reduce the national death-row population by nearly one-third if the court approves the remaining cases. Its review of decades of sentencing data also found that Black and Hispanic defendants were more likely to receive death sentences in California.

The announcement brought strong reactions from both sides. Some prosecutors, police groups and relatives of murder victims said a blanket action ignored the facts of individual crimes.

Civil-rights organizations and other survivors supported the move, pointing to racial disparities, wrongful convictions and the long waits built into the appeals process.

Jess Nichol, whose sister Polly Klaas was murdered in 1993, said execution had “absolutely nothing to do with my recovery.” Newsom said he also understood why other families would strongly disagree.

The commutations do not abolish California’s death penalty. Voters would have to remove it through a ballot measure, and prosecutors can still seek death sentences.

Incoming Governor Xavier Becerra has said he will continue the execution moratorium, leaving the larger law in place while the court reviews Newsom’s requests.

item.title: Molly Santana Launches Black Punk Music Through Epic Records Deal
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Molly Santana signed with Epic Records through Black Punk Music, giving her imprint a home for its next chapter.
item.content:encoded:
Molly Santana has signed a deal with Epic Records through her own Black Punk Music imprint.

The deal gives the 22-year-old rapper a major-label partner without pushing her new venture into the background.

The arrangement creates two connected lanes. Santana joins Epic as an artist, while Black Punk Music becomes the banner for the next stage of her work.

Her first release under the deal, “A Girl Is a Gun,” arrived Friday, November 6.

“Black Punk Music marks a new chapter in my career, one devoted to pushing the boundaries of creativity in music and beyond,” Santana told Billboard.

She said Epic gave the imprint the right home and credited the company with sharing her interest in moving music forward. Epic chairman and CEO Ezekiel Lewis described Santana as an artist with a distinct sound and point of view.

He said the label was ready to support the statement behind Black Punk.

The deal follows a busy year for Santana. Her profile grew after she appeared with Drake and Future on “Ran to Atlanta.”

The song opened at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100. She also released solo records including “Live Your Life” and “Can’t Touch This.” Black Punk Music was already appearing in the release credits.

That run gave the new partnership momentum, but it also arrived after a disrupted summer. Santana and North West announced the Kimokawaii tour in June. The nine-city run was then shelved without a public explanation before its scheduled opening.

Santana released “Molly & Her Week of Wonders” in 2025. The new agreement puts Black Punk Music between that independent rise and a wider Epic system whose rap roster includes Future, Travis Scott and 21 Savage.

The imprint’s name also signals that Santana wants the partnership to carry more than one album campaign.

She framed Black Punk Music as a creative platform, while Epic presented the deal as backing an artist who already knows the direction she wants to take.

Neither Santana nor Epic has announced a release date for her next full-length project. For now, “A Girl Is a Gun” is the first finished release tied to the deal. Black Punk Music has moved from a name in the credits to the center of her business plan.

item.title: BREAKING: Keffe D Attorney Michael Sanft Dies After Tupac Murder Trial
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Michael Sanft, who represented Keffe D in Tupac Shakur's murder trial, has died as the convicted man prepares an appeal.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Sanft, the Las Vegas attorney who represented Duane “Keffe D” Davis during the Tupac Shakur murder trial, has died, according to FOX5 Vegas.

The station reported Sanft’s death through sources. A cause of death was not included in the available report, and no additional circumstances were disclosed.

Sanft became one of the most visible lawyers in Hip-Hop’s longest-running murder case when he joined Davis’ defense team months before trial. He took the case without charging Davis and said his goal was to challenge the prosecution’s evidence without being limited by the family’s ability to pay.

The veteran attorney stepped into a case with material collected across several police agencies and the FBI. His team had only months to prepare for a trial involving decades of interviews, books, recordings and competing accounts of the shooting.

Davis was the only person charged in the 1996 drive-by shooting that killed Tupac Shakur. The rapper was shot near the Las Vegas Strip after leaving a Mike Tyson fight and died six days later at age 25.

The case finally went to trial in August. Prosecutors argued Davis helped organize the attack and provided the gun used in the shooting. The defense maintained that his public accounts were exaggerated stories that could not be trusted as proof of murder.

A jury rejected that argument and convicted Davis of first-degree murder. Sanft said afterward that the jurors moved too quickly through a large record and that the defense planned to challenge the result.

Judge Carli Kierny later sentenced Davis to 40 years to life. The sentence made the expected appeal the next phase of a case that had already stretched across three decades.

Sanft’s death leaves an immediate question about who will handle that work. Davis still has the right to pursue post-conviction review, but any change in counsel will require the new lawyer to absorb a large trial record and the arguments Sanft intended to raise.

No replacement attorney had been identified in the available reporting, and no briefing schedule was available. The court record will show how Davis’ representation changes as the appeal process moves forward.

item.title: Washington And Colorado Voters Approve Transgender Athlete Restrictions
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Washington and Colorado approved school-sports limits for transgender athletes, extending the policy into two Democratic-led states.
item.content:encoded:
Voters in Washington and Colorado approved ballot measures restricting transgender athletes in school sports, taking a policy associated with Republican-led states into two states controlled by Democrats.

Washington’s Initiative 638 was receiving roughly 57 percent support in the state’s unofficial count. Colorado’s Proposition 134 passed with about 53 percent, according to preliminary results. Officials in both states were still completing the canvass, but the races had been called.

The Washington measure bars students it defines as biologically male from competing in female-only K-12 athletic events.

Students seeking to join girls’ teams must submit a signed statement from a health-care provider verifying sex through reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels.

Colorado’s measure reaches K-12 schools and colleges. It requires teams to be designated male, female or coeducational and generally limits athletes to teams matching their sex as defined by reproductive biology. It allows a female athlete to join a male team if no female team is offered.

Supporters framed both campaigns around competitive fairness and athletic opportunities for girls. Brian Heywood, founder of the group behind Washington’s initiative, called the result a victory for girls whose “voices and opportunities don’t matter” to the state’s majority party.

Opponents warned that the rules could expose transgender students and other girls to invasive scrutiny. Colorado advocate Nadine Bridges said a girl who is “too tall or too strong” could face questions about whether she is transgender.

The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association said it knew of roughly 10 transgender students participating in school sports statewide before the vote.

Opponents argued that the small number showed the initiative targeted a vulnerable group. Supporters said a statewide rule was needed before disputes became more common.

The results are politically significant because lawmakers in Washington and Colorado had not adopted the restrictions through their Democratic-led legislatures. Supporters instead put the issue directly before voters.

More than half of U.S. states already have some form of transgender-athlete restriction, although courts have blocked or narrowed some policies.

Washington election officials stressed that results remain unofficial until certification on December 3.

“The results reported on election night are just the beginning,” Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said as counties continued to verify signatures and count ballots.

Colorado’s governor-elect, Phil Weiser, signaled that implementation could face scrutiny. “I don’t believe it would be acceptable” to subject every student athlete to full-body examinations or similar privacy invasions, he said after the election.

The measures now move from campaigns into rulemaking, where schools, athletic associations and state agencies will determine how eligibility is verified and enforced. Legal challenges are also possible as courts continue weighing similar restrictions around the country.

item.title: Stephanie Mills Backs Beyonce In Debate Over Modern Singers
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Stephanie Mills praised Beyonce on "Club Shay Shay" while disagreeing with Chaka Khan's view of modern singers' stage performances.
item.content:encoded:
Stephanie Mills backed Beyonce when Shannon Sharpe asked whether modern singers used their bodies to make up for weak voices.

“I don’t agree with that,” Mills said on the November 4 episode of “Club Shay Shay.” “I think that they follow the queen bee, Beyonce, who is definitely the queen.”

Mills added, “She can do all of that.” She still had reservations about sexual lyrics and twerking. She said newer artists had their own styles and could not be expected to perform like her generation. Mills said she would not dismiss their work.

Sharpe had asked about Chaka Khan’s criticism of modern performers. Khan made those remarks on “Table Manners” in March, when host Jessie Ware raised a discussion about singers putting their voices ahead of elaborate stage production.

“These women are doing any and every damn thing on stage and trying to sing, too,” Khan said. She argued that some performers leaned on physical routines to cover shortcomings. The criticism concerned newer performers in general.

Mills and Khan had shared a stage themselves. The two joined Patti LaBelle and Gladys Knight for “The Queens! 4 Legends. 1 Stage” tour.

For Mills, the point of pride was what the women could still do with their voices. Asked about the tour’s biggest reward in her May BLACK ENTERPRISE interview, she said, “That we’re all still singing in our original keys.”

“I was telling them that we are survivors of this business,” Mills said. Her own path included the original Broadway production of “The Wiz” and major-label recording deals. She later started JM Records to control her releases. “I have my own label,” she said.

She also said she chose songs around the audience. Hits were part of the set, but the album tracks fans liked mattered too.

item.title: Awkwafina Turns Family Restaurant History Into A Culinary Gamble
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Awkwafina learned to cook and staged a one-night Lum's pop-up while weighing a permanent revival of her family's Queens restaurant.
item.content:encoded:
Awkwafina has turned her family’s restaurant history into a real business test, learning to cook and staging a one-night version of Lum’s while she decides whether the Queens institution can live again.

The actor, comedian and rapper documents the process in the eight-episode Apple TV series “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” which premiered Friday. The show follows Nora Lum from basic kitchen lessons to menu planning, staffing and the pressure of serving guests.

Her starting point was blunt. “I can’t cook. Like, at all,” she admits in Apple’s official trailer announcement.

Lum’s was a Cantonese restaurant Awkwafina’s great-grandfather opened in Flushing during the 1950s. The family business closed in 1982, before she was born, but its place in the family never disappeared.

Awkwafina told The Guardian that relatives speak about it “like a family member that passed away.”

That history carried risk as well as pride. Awkwafina said her grandmother later ran her own restaurant.

When it failed, her grandparents filed for bankruptcy and lost their business and home. The family spent a period in a one-bedroom apartment. Those memories give the new project stakes beyond nostalgia.

The series sends her to the Culinary Institute of America and across the country. She studies Texas barbecue with Jimmy O. Yang, learns from Roy Choi and Martin Yan, explores the Hawaiian influences behind her family’s menu and works in a Los Angeles Chinatown restaurant.

Those lessons lead to a Manhattan pop-up built around dishes tied to Lum’s, including barbecue ribs, chow mein, Peking duck and a pupu platter. Her grandmother, who helped raise her, became the night’s most important guest.

The show does not hand Awkwafina a finished concept. It follows basic lessons, menu research, service work, branding and the search for a location and staff. The pop-up becomes a practical test of whether a personal tribute can handle the daily pressure of a restaurant.

The experience changed more than Awkwafina’s television resume. She told The Associated Press that cooking is “a world that you can step into anytime.”

She has since started making meals for herself, including omelets and soup.

A permanent Lum’s has not been announced. Asked whether the pop-up could become something lasting, Awkwafina said the idea is “still in the works of being figured out.”

For now, the restaurant exists as a completed one-night experiment and a family story she has put back in motion.
